# Decision making with conflicting information: influencing factors and best practice guidelines

Meredith B. Carroll and Paige L. Sanchez

College of Aeronautics, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL, USA

## ABSTRACT

As mobile and sensor technology become more prevalent, performers across a range of tasks have access to redundant information sources with the potential to provide conflicting information. There is currently not a consolidated body of literature that examines decision making with conflicting information and there is a need to understand what factors influence this decision-making process. The aim of this effort was to integrate findings from the literature, across a range of domains such as aviation, medical, and military, that examined how individuals make decisions when faced with conflicting information, and to provide practical guidance for optimizing decision making in these circumstances. System factors of reliability, transparency, and workload; individual factors of experience, system trust, and training; and task/ environment factors of time pressure, risk, take-action tendency, type of conflict, and task difficulty were shown to be influencing factors. This paper provides a first step towards understanding this decision making process and guidelines to promote effective decision making in increasingly information-rich environments. Applying these guidelines will help provide performers, ranging from pilots to medical practitioners, with the knowledge and tools they need to assimilate information from multiple sources, accurately assess the situation, and make effective decisions.

**ARTICLE HISTORY**

Accepted 30 April 2020

**KEYWORDS** NE

Decision making; conflicting information; uncertainty; trust; information integration; system design

## Relevance to human factors/Relevance to ergonomics theory

The human factors associated with individuals responding to conflicting information are not currently well understood. This paper puts forth a framework of factors which influence human performance under these circumstances. This framework can serve as a foundation for human factors researchers to explore this problem space and identify solutions for optimizing decision making, across a range of domains, in which individuals are required to assimilate information from an array of sources and make effective decisions.

## Introduction

As mobile and sensor technology become more prevalent, individuals have access to greater amounts of information to assist them in performing a range of different tasks. Pilots now have access to Electronic Flight Bag (EFB) applications that provide them with supplementary weather, traffic and navigation information. Medical practitioners have access to mobile technology and diagnostic equipment that provide assistance in identifying medical anomalies. Unmanned Aircraft System (UAS) operators have access to advanced sensors that provide information on aircraft system status and ground target locations. Although these sources provide additional information to assist in task performance, this information may not be useful if not effectively assimilated (Endsley 2001). Multiple sources of redundant information often have slightly different methods by which the information is obtained, creating the potential for systems to simultaneously present conflicting information. Performers must reconcile, make sense of, and make decisions based on this redundant, and sometimes conflicting information, often with limited knowledge of how the information is obtained and associated levels of accuracy and reliability. For example, UAS pilots report experiencing conflicting information on a daily basis, including up to three different sources of weather and various sources of intelligence that are not always accurate and up-to-date (S. Bennett, personal communication, June 28, 2018). Commercial pilots report experiencing conflicting information between their onboard weather radar and the Next Generation Weather Radar (NEXRAD), where one source shows a significantly different weather outlook than the other. (Carroll et al., 2019). Nurses in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) now have access to real-time heart, urine analysis, and activity monitoring data that has the potential to provide conflicting information that nurses must integrate in order to make medical care decisions (P. Quartz, personal communication, July 6, 2018).

Conflicting information has been shown to have deleterious effects on decision making including reduction in accuracy of decisions, longer decision times and less confidence that the decision was correct (Mosier et al. 2007; Chen and Li 2015). In order to better support performers across a range of domains, it is critical to understand the decision-making process that takes place when an individual is faced with conflicting information. Further, what are the factors that influence which pieces of information performers are more likely to trust and utilize? How can information systems be designed to support appropriate information integration? There is currently not a consolidated body of literature that examines how individuals make decisions with conflicting information. The goal of this research effort is to integrate findings from the literature across a range of domains in order to develop a framework of factors that influence how individuals make decisions when faced with conflicting information. Further, the effort aimed to provide recommendations for optimizing decision making in these circumstances.

## Methods

We conducted a review of the literature across multiple domains to determine what empirical research has revealed about how individuals make decisions when faced with conflicting information, and what factors influence which information individuals are more likely to trust and utilize. The operational need for this research came from the aviation domain, and therefore a significant portion of the literature reviewed concerned aviation. However, literature from other performance domains, such as military, medical, and nuclear, was also included.

First, the research team compiled a list of keywords that were relevant to decision making in the presence of conflicting, redundant, incongruent, or uncertain information. The primary keywords included the main aviation systems and fields of interest, and the secondary keywords were related to conflicting, disparate, and incongruent information, and uncertainty. The keyword list can be found in Table 1. Using the list of keywords, we performed an extensive keyword search of databases such as EBSCO, Google Scholar, ProQuest, Psych Info, and Sage Journals. Additionally, we acquired relevant publications through reference sections of relevant articles and from a “cited by” list search. We initially reviewed 300 abstracts, selected 98 of the publications for a more thorough review, and deemed a total of 51 publications relevant. This included 36 empirical studies and 15 theoretical publications.

Next, we categorized the findings from the 36 empirical studies based on target domain and type of decision. The majority of the studies focused on four different target domains: Aviation, Military, Medical, and Nuclear. The decisions on which these studies focused were then categorized into seven different types of decisions. Aviation decisions with conflicting information fell into three categories: 1) problem diagnosis, 2) traffic collision avoidance, and 3) weather-related decision making. Military decisions fell into the fourth category: tactical decision making, such as identifying enemy targets under conditions of missing, ambiguous, or conflicting information. Medical decisions fell into the fifth category: medical diagnoses of diseases or determining which medication to prescribe with differing levels of information consistency. Nuclear power plant decisions fell into the sixth category: problem diagnosis and decision to act when faced with conflicting or missing information during power plant anomaly or failure situations. The seventh category was an “other” decision category which included studies not related to these domains, but that required participants to diagnose a failure or problem within a system when faced with conflicting information. The decision categories for each domain and example decisions are summarized in Table 2.

Finally, based on the level of corroboration across the 36 empirical publications, we quantified, prioritized, and summarized findings from the studies, resulting in two primary outcomes: 1) a framework of factors, shown through multiple studies, to influence decision making with conflicting information, and 2) best practice guidelines for supporting effective decision making with conflicting information. The 15 theoretical publications provided theoretical background to help interpret the empirical studies and recommend mitigation strategies. Additional publications, beyond those identified in the initial review of the literature, were identified and incorporated during the development of this manuscript.

## Results

## The decision making process

There are multiple areas of research in the literature that can help shed light on the decision making process that occurs when an individual is faced with conflicting information. In particular, research into naturalistic decision making with complex systems is an area in which this phenomenon has been studied. For example, Lipshitz and Strauss (1997) studied military decision making with uncertainty by collecting narratives from military officers associated with cases of decision making under uncertainty. The researchers identified three distinct types of uncertainty in decision making, one of which was conflicting information, and five different coping strategies utilized to make decisions under these different circumstance (Lipshitz and Strauss 1997). Analysis of these cases led to development of the R.A.W.F.S. Heuristic, which describes, in detail, how performers make decisions under conditions of uncertainty. The key attributes of the R.A.W.F.S. Heuristic are that decision-makers first attempt to make sense of the situation, which if successful leads to evaluation of different options and ultimately a choice. However, if this step is unsuccessful, decision-makers typ ically collect additional information in an attempt to reduce the uncertainty. If additional information is not available, they make assumptions, weigh pros and cons among alternatives, ignore undesirable information if no consensus is reached, act early to get ahead of the situation, and generate new alternatives in order to move forward with selecting a decision alternative. Lipshitz and Strauss also found that when faced with conflicting information, decision makers were most likely to respond by weighing pros and cons. This is consistent with interview data collected from a small sample of pilots which indicated that when faced with conflicting information, pilots typically collected additional information and consider the strengths and weaknesses of each source of information (Carroll et al. 2019).

Endsley and Jones (2004) present a discussion of decision making with uncertainty, including conflicting information, and propose six strategies that decision makers utilize to reduce uncertainty. Endsley and Jones propose that decision makers respond to uncertainty by (a) collecting additional information, (b) replacing missing information with default values based on their active mental model, (c) actively working to resolve and information conflict, (d) proceeding with what they believe is an acceptable amount of uncertainty, (e) planning for the worst case scenario, and (f) working to narrow the possibilities of what can occur in a situation. Decision makers are proposed to actively work to resolve information conflicts by attempting to determine which source of information is correct based on which information source could be erroneous. If this is not fruitful, decision makers consider all information sources while taking into account source reliabilities.

This decision making process is shaped by a range of different factors related to the individual performer and the situation in which the decision occurs. The following section presents a framework of factors that influence this decision process and reviews the literature associated with each of these factors.

## A framework of factors that influence decision making with conflicting information

Figure 1 presents a framework of factors, shown through multiple studies, to influence how individuals make decisions when faced with conflicting information. These influencing factors, which are unique but not independent, fall into three categories: 1) System Factors related to characteristics of the system in use, 2) Individual Factors related to characteristics of the performer, and 3) Task/Environmental Factors related to the task being performed or the environment in which it is performed.

## System factors

We found three system factors that were consistently shown to impact how an individual responds when faced with redundant or conflicting information: (1) reliability, (2) trans parency, and (3) workload. We acknowledge that the impact that these factors have on system interaction is not a novel finding and that they are associated with basic system design principles; however, our goal is to consolidate and highlight the factors that appear to be most influential when a decision maker is faced with conflicting information.

## Reliability

System reliability was the most prominent system factor in the literature shown to impact decision making with conflicting information. The literature suggests that performers tend to have greater trust in, and utilize more often, those systems with the highest reported, experienced, or perceived reliability (Bahner, Huper, and Manzey 2008; Wickens and Dixon 2007; Skitka 1999; Bolstad and Endsley 1998; Levine and Samet 1973). Skitka (1999) investigated how participants responded when aircraft automation with varying levels of reported reliability (i.e., reported to them by the researchers), conflicted with analog gauges with varying levels of reported reliability, and found that people opted to go with the recommendation that had the greatest probability of being right. Skitka replicated these findings in both automobile and nuclear power plant performance domains, and in both cases, participants made a decision based on the most reliable source. Similarly, in a medical study conducted by Goddard (2012), when the participants perceived the reliability of a diagnostic system as high, there was an increased tendency to follow the diagnosis given by the system. In a military study conducted by Levine and Samet (1973), when sources with reportedly high and low reliability were presented in the same scenario, participants defaulted to the source reported to have high reliability.

## Transparency

System transparency, which provides performers an understanding of system logic, can influence performers’ decision making with conflicting information. Systems that provide insight into system algorithms and alerting thresholds support performers in effectively evaluating the commands in the face of an information conflict (Pritchett 1998). Systems which do not provide this insight can leave performers questioning system effectiveness. Song and Kuchar (2001) found that when an operator clearly understands the rationale behind the alerting system’s behaviour, conflicting alerts are less likely to confuse, or hinder the operator’s decision making ability. Fleming and Pritchett (2015) found that pilots with an insufficient understanding of the traffic avoidance system’s logic were less likely to both trust and comply with certain types of commands. In a study conducted by Pritchett (1998), pilots were presented automated alerts that conflicted with their mental picture and personal decision. The results indicated that pilots who felt that the automated command was not sufficient to remedy a problem (indicative of their lack of understanding of system logic), determined their own course of action to resolve the problem, or used a modified version that was more severe. Similarly, Pritchett et al. (2012) found that when a pilot received any callout from ATC about an aircraft before an automated traffic command associated with that aircraft, compliance with the automated command was significantly lower. This is likely due to the ATC callout providing transparency into the process that ATC was using to deconflict the aircraft.

## Workload

Workload required to understand information was a factor found to influence decision making with redundant information. Pritchett (1998) found that if an automated system’s command is difficult to understand, increasing the workload, the performer may ignore the alert. Campbell and Alexander (2016) found that although pilots find it easier to avoid weather with big-picture information such as a graphical weather display, a simple textbased notification, which may require less workload, resulted in quicker decision times to initiate action (Campbell and Alexander 2016). This aligns with findings from a medical study conducted by Law et  al. (2005), in which neonatal ICU staff made more correct decisions when presented with medical scenarios summarized textually compared to scenarios presented as a set of trend graphs. This was hypothesized to be due to the workload required to interpret the graphs.

## Individual factors

We found three individual factors that were shown in the literature to impact how an individual responds when faced with conflicting information: (1) experience, (2) system trust, and (3) training.

## Experience

Experience was the most heavily cited individual factor that influences decision making with conflicting information. Experience has positive impacts in these situations, including increased decisiveness (St John et al. 2000) and reduced decision time (Khoo and Mosier 2005). There is also evidence to suggest that as experience increases, individuals may have a more discerning eye regarding which information is more relevant. For instance, the results of a medical study conducted by Tabak, Bar-Tal, and Cohen-Mansfield (1996) indicated that when determining a diagnosis when inconsistent information is present, nursing students tended to ignore inconsistent information more than experienced nurses. Kushniruk (2001) examined the impact of expertise on pulmonary embolism diagnosis based on conflicting information between a report of clinical evidence and an image of a lung scan. Results indicated that in the face of inconsistent information between these two sources, medical students were much more likely to rely on evidence from a lung scan, compared to more traditionally collected clinical evidence. This was true even when the results of the scan showed a low probability of an abnormality. Expert physicians, however, were much more likely to disregard the anomalous information in favour of the overarching clinical picture.

There is evidence, however, to suggest that expertise does not always have a positive impact in these situations. A line of research conducted by Mosier et al. (1998) examined how pilots respond to automated information and commands, often in conflict with a traditional source of information on the flight deck. Mosier et  al. (1998) found that experience, as measured by both number of flight hours and years of flight experience, were positively correlated with number of omission errors (i.e., failing to complete a needed action that was not recommended by the automation), suggesting that experienced pilots tend to trust an automated source of information when in conflict with other sources of information. This is in-line with additional research which has shown that more experienced pilots are more likely to rely on automation in comparison to student pilots, even after an automation failure (Riley 1994). This is proposed to potentially be due to the “phantom memory” phenomenon, in which pilots falsely remember a cue corroborating what the automated source indicates, likely due to their experience with that cue being repeatedly present in highly reliable systems (Mosier et al. 1998; Mosier 2009; Mosier 2002).

## System trust

Trust in the system providing the information can impact how a pilot responds to an information conflict. Evidence suggests that performers who have a greater level of trust in automation tend to follow the automation system’s recommendations and alerts (Skitka, Mosier, and Burdick 1999; Goddard 2012). For example, in a study conducted by Skitka, Mosier, and Burdick (1999) in which performers were sometimes presented with conflicting information, participants who trusted the automated system, perceiving it as highly accurate, were more likely to diffuse responsibility to the automated system when a conflict was present. Similarly, a medical study conducted by Goddard (2012) found that participants who had a greater level of trust in a system tended to follow the system’s diagnosis over their own personal diagnosis of which medication to prescribe to a patient. Lastly, in a study conducted by Pritchett (1998), results showed that when pilots were not confident that the alerting system would generate an alert when required, they were likely to perform their own situation assessment, without the help of the automated system.

## Training

Training was another factor found in the literature to influence decision making under uncertainty. Repetitive training that creates situations similar to actual operating conditions, is a key characteristic that enables effective decision making under uncertain conditions experienced by military commanders (Karaoguz 2016). Similarly, Fleming and Pritchett (2015) found that when pilots were trained in a realistic operating context, they were more likely to consistently comply with traffic avoidance advisories when they were in conflict with ATC guidance. Additionally, pilots who received this type of training more often prevented additional traffic events from occurring, and were less likely to contact ATC for further instructions. Bahner, Huper, and Manzey (2008) found that when participants in a process control simulation were exposed to conflicting information during training, they were more likely to monitor redundant cues and crosscheck automation during an infor mation conflict. Training was also a factor found to impact pilot response to conflicting information between an automated traffic collision avoidance system and ATC in the Uberlingen fatal midair collision (Nunes and Laursen 2004). The European pilot was trained to follow the automated alert in all circumstances; however, the Russian pilot was trained to take both ATC and the automated command into account, resulting in the European pilot following the automated advisory to descend, while the Russian pilot opted to follow ATC’s instructions to also descend.

## Task/environmental factors

We found five factors related to the task or environment that have been shown to impact how an individual responds when faced with redundant or conflicting information: (1) time pressure, (2) risk, (3) take-action tendency, (4) type of conflict, and (5) task difficulty.

## Time pressure

Time pressure was one of the most heavily cited task/environment factors shown to influence how pilots respond when faced with conflicting information. In a study examining pilots’ responses to conflicting information, Mosier et al. (2007) found that pilots under time pressure checked fewer pieces of information and performed fewer double checks of information, resulting in a tendency to miss relevant information and diagnose less accurately under time pressure. Bahner, Huper, and Manzey (2008) found that when participants were in a demanding environment with time pressure, complacency (i.e., inappropriate checking and monitoring of automated functions) effects tended to arise. The researchers concluded that, under time pressure, participants rely more heavily on the automated system and fail to detect and utilize conflicting information. Khoo and Mosier (2005) found that experienced pilots under time pressure were significantly faster than less experienced pilots during the diagnostic process. However, when no time pressure was present, the experienced pilots spent more time verifying information and rechecking cues before making a decision. Lastly, Chen and Li (2015) conducted a nuclear power plant study and found that, under time pressure, in scenarios where there was conflicting information, participants generated fewer hypotheses for consideration in their diagnosis than when they were not under time pressure. The authors concluded that when faced with conflicting information, participants needed to collect additional information to determine which source was more accurate and potentially follow “a new line of logic”; time pressure limited their ability to do this (p. 931).

## Risk

Risk influences which source of conflicting information is utilized. In general, in uncertain situations, people typically act to minimize risk. In a study conducted by Pritchett et al. (2012), pilots were given instructions from ATC shortly before receiving a conflicting automated traffic avoidance command. Results indicated that pilots were more likely to comply with ATC instructions when automated instructions were perceived as high risk (e.g., requiring pilots to fly through the altitude of a climbing intruder aircraft) than instruc tions perceived to have low risk. In a study examining physician decision making when there was incongruent information, physicians tended to continue to generate hypotheses of different potential diagnoses until at least one severe diagnosis with high risk was generated (Weber et al. 1993). In a study conducted by Bliss et al. (2005), researchers found that pilots were more likely to trust the weather display that showed weather activity (i.e., higher risk) than the one that did not, suggesting that when information sources conflict, individuals are more likely to trust the source that shows the presence of a hazard than one that does not.

## Take-action tendency

Take-action tendency is a task factor shown to influence how performers choose to respond in uncertain situations, both independently and in conjunction with risk. In a series of studies examining individual response to conflicting information in aviation, nuclear power plant and automobile domains, Skitka (1999) found that when automation and gauges conflicted, and when they had an equal reliability, participants had a strong preference toward the option that recommended action. If the reliabilities of the automation and gauges were different, many participants preferred the option that recommended action even though the information source had a lower reliability. Skitka also found that participants were more likely to take action when there was high risk associated with doing nothing or being wrong. Participants also had a tendency toward action when the risk associated with the action being taken was low. When there was a high risk associated with the action, the participant tended toward the source with the highest reported reliability, regardless of whether it recommended an action. In a survey-based study, Mosier, Keyes, and Bernhard (2000) presented pilot participants with a series of scenarios in which two sources conflicted, with one source indicating that action should be taken and the other source indicating that the participant should maintain status quo. Mosier, Keyes, and Bernhard found that pilots tended to choose the option that recommended action over inaction, and that the higher the estimated risk of a scenario, the more likely pilots were to choose action, and the more confident they were in their choice.

## Type of conflict

Type of conflict, that is, whether information from a source was directly in conflict with one or multiple sources, or information from one source was missing or ambiguous, was another factor shown to influence how performers make decisions. In a military study conducted by Shattuck, Miller, and Kemmerer (2009), the results showed that decision makers tended to respond more slowly to situations with ambiguous and missing information, compared to situations in which the information was directly in conflict. Another military study conducted by Lipshitz and Strauss (1997), found that decision makers use different strategies to cope with different types of information conflicts. When faced with directly conflicting information, decision makers most often weigh pros and cons and choose among alternatives based on potential gains and losses. When there was an inadequate understanding of the situation, decision makers generally collected additional information to reduce uncertainty, or defer decisions. When faced with incomplete information, performers generally extrapolate information, making assumptions that go beyond what is currently known until new information is available. Similarly, Chen and Li (2015) nuclear power plant diagnosis study found that participants spent more time generating a correct hypothesis and rated the accuracy of their results with lower probability for a scenario in which there was directly conflicting information compared to a scenario in which information from one source was missing. In fact, there was no significant difference between how participants responded to scenarios in which there was missing information, compared to scenarios in which all information was congruent, suggesting that participants likely assumed that the missing data was not in conflict. Bolstad and Endsley found similar results in a study that examined individual’s response to both conflicting and missing information in a simulated aircraft defense task (1998). Results indicated that participants treated missing data as if it were congruent with other sensors; however, dissonant data that was in conflict with other sensors led to negative performance impacts.

Gilson et  al. (2001) conducted a series of studies examining individual response to multiple ambiguous, and potentially conflicting, alarms in a generic annunciator panel. Results indicated that operator confidence in, and response to, alarms is impacted by an array of factors including the number of active and inactive alarms present, distances between alarms, and when the alarms were triggered. The greater the percentage of alarms that were activated (i.e., the fewer the inactive alarms that were seemingly in conflict), the more confident in, and more likely was the operator to respond to, the alarm. Further, alarms in close proximity, either temporally or spatially, had a greater impact compared to those less proximal; suggesting operators inferred a relatedness based on both spatial and temporal proximity.

## Task difficulty

Perceived task difficulty was a factor cited as influencing how individuals respond to conflicting information. Skitka, Mosier, and Burdick (1999) found that when a conflict was present between automated information and traditional gauges and pilots perceived the task as easy, they were more likely to take the advice of the automation. Interestingly, in Goddard’s (2012) medical study, task difficulty impacted decision making in a different way. Participants were more likely to experience higher decision switching (switching their initial prescription decision to follow the advice of the unreliable automated system) when they encountered more difficult prescribing scenarios. Task difficulty also impacted decision confidence, wherein decision confidence was significantly lower when the scenario was difficult. The difference in decision making responses across these studies may be due to the differences associated with the aviation and medical domains. There are typically higher levels of standardization of information displays across aircraft compared to medical equipment (Kapur et al. 2016). Additionally, pilots are typically trained and undergo proficiency checks using simulators and are heavily trained in non-technical skills such as information integration, allowing pilots to become familiar with the automated systems and how to handle conflicting information. On the other hand, simulators are generally less used in medical training, and training non-technical skills has become more prevalent only in recent years (Kapur et al. 2016).

## Factor interactions

Although the factors reported in the previous sections are unique constructs, they are not necessarily independent. Several of the factors are highly correlated or interact to impact decision making with conflicting information. For example, system trust has been shown to be highly dependent on system reliability in a range of settings (Chavaillaz, Wastell, and Saucer, 2016; Ross et al. 2008; Chugh and Caird 1999). Task difficulty and time pressure are highly related to workload (Galy, Cariou, and Mélan 2012). Further, system reliability has been shown to interact with type of information conflict and level of risk. When information is in conflict, performers have been shown to make decisions based on the most reliable information source; however, when a source of information is missing, reliability appears to play less of a role as performers were shown to rely more on the number of sources in agreement (Bolstad and Endlsey 1998). Risk has also been shown to interact with take-action tendency. Performers have a greater tendency towards action when the situation is high risk (Skitka 1999; Mosier, Keyes, and Bernhard 2000). Further, when there is a high risk associated with the action, participants tended toward the source with the highest reported reliability, regardless of whether it recommended an action. Experience and time pressure have also been shown to interact. Specifically, more experienced pilots have been shown to make decisions more quickly than novices under time pressure; however, when given unlimited time to make a decision, experienced pilots took longer checking and cross-checking to ensure an effective decision (Khoo and Mosier 2005). Given these dependencies, there may not always be a clear-cut relationship between each of the factors and the impact on decision making with conflicting information.

## Best practice guidelines

It is often challenging for individuals to make effective decisions when faced with conflicting information. However, the literature provides us with a range of methods that can be used to help mitigate the negative effects of information conflicts and promote effective decision making. Integrating techniques recommended for coping with uncertainty (Endsley and Jones 2004), general interaction design principles (Preece, Sharp, and Rogers 2019) and recommendations identified from our literature review, we present here several best practice guidelines for system and training design. These recommendations aim to provide decision makers the tools and training they need to make effective decisions when faced with conflicting information.

## System-design guidelines

There are multiple ways that systems can be designed to support decision makers when faced with conflicting information.

1. Provide indication of uncertainty. Displays should include information regarding the level of certainty associated with different sources of redundant information. This can be provided utilizing numerical or graphical indications of reliability, recency or signal strength. Providing information regarding reliability can help decision makers determine which source is likely the most accurate when faced with an information conflict, and act accordingly. There are several ways this can be accomplished. Endsley and Jones (2004) suggest displaying reliability information either numerically, or with techniques such as varying luminance levels as reliability varies (e.g., highest luminance associated with most reliable sources). Numerical and graphical techniques for displaying information probabilities have been shown to have positive impacts on decision making across multiple tasks with varying information reliability (Finger and Bisantz 2002; Antifakos et al. 2005) . Graphical display of probability, such as the use of degraded images, has been shown to result in quicker decision times; however, with less conservative decisions (i.e., reliance on information with lower confidence levels; Finger and Bisantz 2002). Information that can assist the decision maker in assessing the reliability of the information would also be beneficial to the user (Endsley and Jones 2004); for example displaying information regarding recency or associated signal strength.

2. Increase system transparency and feedback. System transparency can assist a performer in making an effective decision when faced with conflicting information. The literature suggests that systems should provide insight into underlying logic, rationale, and cause and effect of alarms, alerts, and information given to the operator (Gilson, Deaton, and Mouloua 1996; Goddard 2012; Fleming and Pritchett 2015; Mosier et al. 2007. This will allow the pilot to more effectively compare and weigh the conflicting information (Pritchett 1998). Providing decision makers with information regarding the logic behind automated systems has shown to facilitate appropriate levels of trust in multi-ple studies in an aviation piloting context (Lyons et  al. 2016, 2017). In addition to providing information about system logic, feedback should be provided regarding what actions have been taken by the system and what has been accomplished as a result. This is a basic design principle (Preece, Sharp, and Rogers 2019). Providing feedback about the system status and behaviour will allow the operator to be able to more appropriately respond to conflicting information (Mosier et al. 1998).

3. Present the right type of information, in the right format. Display prompts and information should be simple and easy to interpret while encouraging verification to protect the operator from decision making biases (Mosier et al. 1998; Goddard 2012). This can reduce the workload associated with consuming the information. Methods for simplifying information include 1) using straight forward language, and 2) minimizing the amount and complexity of information conveyed. Recent trends are to use graphical displays to reduce complexity of information; however, caution must be taken because this results in an intuitive interpretation. For tasks that require a performer to maintain coherence amongst conflicting information, digital and numerical displays may actually be more effective (Mosier 2002); however, there is equivocal evidence to support this (Endlsey and Jones 2004). For example, displays that present categorical data (e.g. high, medium, low) have been shown to lead to increased decision times compared to numerical displays; however, numerical displays in other circumstances have had positive results, as have other types of displays such auditory and haptic displays (Endlsey and Jones 2004). Making numerical/textual data available with graphical data may be a good option to improve decision making, especially for situations in which the data is meant to signal the performer to take action (Campbell and Alexander 2016). Consideration should also be given to the amount of precision utilized in presenting information, as unnecessary levels of precision may lead to decreased decision times (Endsley and Jones 2004).

Optimize saliency. Saliency can be utilized in two key ways when designing to support decision makers that are likely to be faced with conflicting information. First, saliency can be utilized to promote the use of more reliable pieces of information. Endsley and Jones (2004) suggest placing the most reliable sources of information in the most prominent places to encourage use. Second, salience can also be used to promote equal use of multiple sources of information with similar levels of reliability. Displays could be designed so that competing information (e.g., redundant information from two different, yet reliable sources) is made equally salient (Mosier, Keyes, and Bernhard 2000). Methods for equalizing saliency include ensuring that one information source is not 1) located in a more prominent location (e.g., closer to performer, more centrally located), 2) larger, or 3) presented with brighter or more conspicuous colors.

5. Use attentional cueing. When redundant information is presented on the flight deck, attentional cueing (e.g., highlighting, pointing cues) can be used to attract users’ attention to relevant information, such as redundant information sources that should be considered (Sarter, Woods, and Billings 1997; Mosier et al. 2007). This can also aid in reducing the workload associated with searching for verification information. However, care must be taken, as cueing can have unintended consequences by acting as an attentional trap. For example, cueing symbology presented in a head-mounted display (HMD) was found to increase target detection of cued and expected targets, but this came at the expense of missing un-cued targets, likely due to the attentional trap (Yeh, Wickens, and Seagull 1999). However, the researchers found that this cost was significantly reduced when utilized on a handheld display which was more similar to a traditional panel-mounted cockpit display than an HMD. However, consideration should be taken in ensuring any attentional cues do not detract attention from critical, non-cued information.

6. Provide decision support. The system should guide the user to relevant information, assist them in making their own informed recommendations, and manage recommendations given by the system (Mosier et al. 2007; Mosier and Fischer 2010). This may include “roadmaps for locating relevant information, tracking system recommendations” and “interpreting and verifying their recommendations” (Mosier et al. 2007, p. 309; Mosier and Fischer 2010, p. 237). This can help operators determine whether their decision making process is appropriate and accurate (Mosier and Fischer 2010). For instance, the system can prompt the user to “check system parameters, look for disconfirming evidence, and consider the consequences of an action” (Mosier and Fischer 2010, p. 239). Endsley and Jones (2004) suggest explicitly iden tifying missing information to ensure that operators consider this piece of information and not just assume it is congruent with other sources of information. The system’s display prompts should also encourage verification throughout the decision-making process (Mosier et al. 1998).

## Training-design guidelines

There are also multiple ways that training can be designed to ensure performers have the knowledge and skills they need to make effective decisions when faced with conflicting information.

1. Increase experience with information conflicts. Continuous exposure to new situations of uncertainty and conflicting information, characterized by realistic and simulated operating conditions, can help lead to effective decision making (Franke 2011; Fleming and Pritchett 2015; Karaoguz 2016). During these simulated trainings, performers should be exposed to rare false information so that they gain experience in analysing and reacting to misinformation, in order to improve pilots’ awareness of the possible discrepancies that they may encounter on the flight deck (Bahner, Huper, and Manzey 2008). Case studies, analogies, and thinking aloud can be incorporated into training to help build this experience base (Tabak, Bar-Tal, and Cohen-Mansfield 1996). Performers can also learn how to handle information conflicts from more experienced pilots, by including training methods that promote dialog between novice and experienced pilots, where pilots can learn directly from the experiences and decisions of others through observation, reading first-person accounts, or by directly communicating with the experienced pilots (Tabak, Bar-Tal, and Cohen-Mansfield 1996; Karaoguz 2016). It should be noted; however, that past research has indicated that simply warning performers of possible systems failures, that could, for example, result in conflicting information being presented, may not be sufficient to change performance strategies (Skitka et al. 2000). However, actual exposure to such failures has been shown to influence trust and utilization of information to make decisions (Dzindolet et al. 2003).

2. Train information integration skills. Performers should be trained to evaluate redundant cues in context with all other cues, and training should encourage performers to verify automated functioning with other sources of information (Mosier et  al. 1998; Mosier, Keyes, and Bernhard 2000; Khoo and Mosier 2005). Training for thorough information search and diagnosis, in an information-redundant environment will improve the ability of performers to maintain a logical understanding of the current state of the environment (Mosier 2002). Training should also teach inductive techniques to resolve conflicts, such as envisioning missing alerts resulting from sensor failures (Gilson, Deaton, and Mouloua 1996). Research has indicated that exposure to information conflicts on the flight deck increased pilot crosschecking; however, it was often accompanied by reduced confidence, an affect the authors attribute to pilots not realizing the criticality of thorough information search (Mosier et al. 2007). This suggests it is critical to ensure information search is targeted in training.

3. Train functional system knowledge. Operators should be trained in how their systems work at a functional level (Mosier and Fischer 2010). If operators are aware of the functional operations of a system and the system’s limitations (e.g., reliability), they will be better able to diagnose unexpected problems, monitor more effectively, and determine optimal solutions during situations of uncertainty (Gilson, Deaton, and Mouloua 1996; Mosier and Fischer 2010). Training should focus on improving a pilot’s ability to distinguish true and false alarms (Gilson, Deaton, and Mouloua 1996; Woods and Sarter 2000) and focus on pilots developing an effective, balanced, and unbiased mental model of information source strengths and weaknesses, enabling operators to reliably discriminate trustworthy from untrustworthy information (Sarter, Woods, and Billings 1997; Mosier et al. 2007; Richter and Maier 2017).

4. Train decision strategies and biases. Decision training should not only focus on teaching analytical methods where a best option is “calculated” based on objective, resources and information, but also how to understand complexities of a situation, and recall and utilize heuristics that worked well in the past. This type of strategic decision training must be repetitive and varied, as trainees will need to learn how to recall heuristics that worked and didn’t work across a range of situations (Franke 2011). Phillips, Klein, and Sieck (2004) propose that decision training should strive to develop, within the decision maker, a “large and varied repertoire of patterns” of situations for which they can develop strategies to respond, and that “carefully designed decision scenarios combined with coaching” regarding how to respond in these situations has been shown effective (p. 307).

Decision training could also incorporate education on decision biases and associated mitigation strategies (Parasurman and Riley 1997). There are several decision making biases that humans commonly exhibit, such as anchoring bias (i.e., the tendency to trust the first piece of information received), saliency bias (i.e., the tendency towards the most conspicuous piece of information received), take-action tendency (i.e., the tendency to take action instead of maintaining status quo), sunk-cost bias (the tendency to persist in a failing course of action because time has been invested), and confirmation bias (i.e., the tendency to only look for information that confirms your current diagnosis of the situation; Vidulich et al. 2010). Nickerson (1998) presents fairly comprehensive and compelling evidence regarding the role that confirmation bias plays in almost everything we do: individuals tend to look primarily for information that supports their previously held perceptions and often only consider one hypothesis regarding a situation and assume it is true. These tendencies have been shown to impact decision making with conflicting information. Maier and Richter (2013) examined reader response to conflicting information regarding a controversial issues such as global warming and found information that was consistent with a reader’s preconceived opinions and schema were more likely to shape their ultimate decision regarding what they believed to be true.

Although early research examining the success of decision bias training, or “debiasing training”, has had equivocal results, more recent research is promising. Morewedge et al. (2015) conducted two longitudinal experiments in which participants received debiasing training on multiple biases relevant to intelligence analysis (e.g., confirmation bias) and found that debiasing training significantly reduced decision biases, across different contexts, that persisted for two months. Poos, Bosch, and Janssen (2017) also found debiasing training which utilized interactive and text-based games to reduce confirmation bias and attribution error bias to be successful. However, earlier experiments, such as those designed to debias hindsight biases, have not been found successful (Sanna, Schwarz, and Stocker 2002).

5. Train self-reflection skills. Training should also target self-reflection skills such as metacognition, or the “monitoring and control of thought” (Martinez 2006, p. 696). Metacognitive skills, which could prove helpful when making decisions marked by conflicting information, include the ability to select an appropriate judgment strategy based on the situation, as well as perform mental simulations, such as playing a potential solution through in one’s head to identify critical risks and relevant situational factors (Mosier and Fischer 2010). Metacognitive training can lead to “more thorough information search, more analytical cognition, and more coherent judgement strategies” (Mosier and Fischer 2010, p. 240), as well as stronger mental models in situations of uncertainty (Richter and Maier 2017).

## Conclusion

As pilots, medical practitioners, UAS operators and beyond are provided with increasing amounts of redundant information, decision making with conflicting information will increasingly become a concern. It is critical to understand how individuals make decisions when faced with conflicting information in order to effectively prepare them and provide the tools necessary for successful task performance. The Federal Aviation Administration is particularly interested in this issue as they work to ensure that NextGen technologies and procedures are reliable and safe, and that the NextGen goals of increased safety, capacity, and efficiency are realized. This paper provides a first step towards this understanding by presenting a framework of factors that impact decision making with conflicting infor mation and recommendations for promoting effective decision making in these circum stances. Future research is needed to further understand this phenomenon in emerging domains, such as augmented reality, in which information conflicts are becoming more prevalent and are bound to impact performance effectiveness.

## Notes on contributors

**Dr. Meredith Carroll** is an Associate Professor of Aviation Human Factors at Florida Institute of Technology’s College of Aeronautics. She has over 15 years of experience studying human/team performance and training in complex systems. Her research focuses on decision making in complex systems, cognition and learning, performance assessment and adaptive training, including utilizing physiological sensor technology to gain access to previously unobservable aspects of performance. She received her B.S. in Aerospace Engineering from the University of Virginia, her Masters in Aviation Science from Florida Institute of Technology and her Ph.D. in Applied Experimental Psychology and Human Factors from the University of Central Florida.

**Paige Sanchez** recently graduated from the Florida Institute of Technology’s College of Aeronautics with her Masters in Aviation Human Factors. Her current research focuses on pilot decision making on the flight deck and the usability and design of information-heavy mobile applications used in safety critical industries. Paige also has experience in research focusing on the crashworthiness of high-performance vehicles, including accident reconstruction, 3 D simulations and stress analysis, understanding the physical interaction between the human body and a racecar, as well as the fabrication and build of a dragster. She has Masters degrees in both Mechanical Engineering and Aviation Human Factors from Florida Institute of Technology and a B.S. in Mechanical Engineering from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University.
